---
name: technical-deprecation
description: Plan, implement, or review retirement of a supported library, API, configuration option, or internal tool when consumers must migrate. Use for replacement readiness, stalled deprecations, and removal gates; exclude private unused-helper cleanup, worker draining, and public-product shutdown policy.
license: MIT
---

# Technical deprecation

Retire a technical contract through evidenced consumer transitions. Keep the
requested scope: review returns findings; planning supplies the next stage;
implementation performs the authorized migration slice. A warning, deadline,
or replacement launch does not establish that removal is safe.

## 1. Define the retirement decision

Name the contract, intended benefit, supported users and versions, governing
compatibility policy, and replacement or explicitly approved withdrawal. Distinguish
discouraging new use from committing to removal. Existing support obligations
continue until the applicable policy changes; age alone supplies no reason to retire.

Identify who owns migration progress and who can accept unresolved consumer risk.
Use actual assignments; if absent, propose the required role and leave its decision
pending while continuing independent inspection. Scale the record to the change.

**Done:** the target, permitted behavior changes, accountable role, and requested
stage are explicit; missing decisions cannot silently become removal approval.

## 2. Establish consumers and replacement readiness

Trace callers and the behavior they rely on. For dependencies outside a closed
local call graph, dynamic use, or quiet usage reports, read
[consumer evidence](references/consumer-evidence.md). Record what each evidence
source covers and which consumers remain unknown.

Compare the replacement against affected consumer contracts: inputs, outputs,
errors, effects, and persisted formats where relevant. Exercise a representative
consumer before bulk migration. Classify each behavior as preserved, deliberately
changed, or unresolved; a renamed method or passing provider test proves little
about a caller's needs.

**Done:** each known consumer has a transition or an explicit unresolved gap,
and required replacement behavior has checks rather than a feature-parity claim.

## 3. Prepare and execute the next migration stage

For warnings, preventing new dependencies, coexistence, or physical removal, read
[migration gates](references/migration-gates.md). Assign the next bounded batch,
its verification, and recovery action. Preserve functioning consumers during the
agreed transition and prevent new usage through a check whose scope is explicit.

Draft any required notices with the affected interface, replacement, supported
transition, owner, and applicable dates; send them only when communication is
authorized. Keep live disabling and external changes within existing task
authorization. Prefer isolated compatibility checks when preparing a retirement.

**Done:** the requested stage is implemented and checked, or its plan names the
owner, acceptance evidence, and stop/recovery condition. Later stages remain plans.

## 4. Verify removal and report the actual state

Reconcile the consumer inventory with migrated behavior and remaining dependency
evidence. A newly discovered caller or unmet replacement requirement stops the
dependent retirement step. Rehearse removal at the affected boundary in an
isolated target; retain a legacy-use control that demonstrates the check's sensitivity.

Report completed migrations, remaining users and visibility gaps, checks actually
run, and the next release/removal gate. Separate ready-to-remove from removed.
If the task ends before retirement, retain an actionable owner and next step rather
than declaring the deprecation complete. Read [sources](references/sources.md)
when checking attribution or applying a platform's policy.

**Done:** each completion claim names its stage and evidence; unresolved consumer,
policy, or recovery conditions remain visible.

# Consumer evidence

Use this branch when usage can escape a closed local caller search. Keep a compact
record for each consumer group: evidence location and revision/time, required
behavior, migration owner, replacement status, and remaining uncertainty.

Choose evidence from the actual exposure:

| Exposure | Evidence to inspect | What it cannot establish alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source dependency | Imports, exports, aliases, build/dependency graph, generated clients | Unavailable repositories or dynamically selected targets |
| Runtime selection | Registries, configuration, plugins, scheduled jobs, fallback paths | An unexecuted branch's absence |
| Deployed clients | Supported versions, release inventory, identified usage | Offline or infrequent callers outside the observation interval |
| Retained inputs | Stored configuration, serialized names, queued work, replay tooling | Compatibility with history that was never sampled |

Label evidence as observed use, covered absence, or unknown. Record which
environments, versions, paths, and time interval were observed. Match an observation
window to the relevant usage cadence; an arbitrary quiet interval cannot rule out
a periodic job. State unavailable consumer access instead of inventing a complete
inventory. Consumer acknowledgement helps locate responsibility but does not
replace a compatibility check.

Select a representative case from each materially different required behavior,
including a fallback or error outcome when migration changes it. Keep equivalent
behavior separate from an authorized product decision to withdraw behavior.
For effectful calls, compare in an isolated fixture or through an explicitly safe
observation path; invoking both implementations against a live target can duplicate
the operation. These evidence categories and checks are repository applications,
not a claim that any one search technique proves every consumer absent.
# Migration and retirement gates

Read the branch matching the requested stage. A small migration needs only its
relevant gates; keep the project's existing issue and release mechanisms.

## Discouraging or blocking new usage

Choose a check at the actual dependency boundary: a build rule, targeted static
check, API policy, or scoped runtime validation. Define whether it prevents new
consumer projects, new call sites, or all use. Preserve explicitly supported legacy
uses while they migrate; record exceptions with an owner and an exit condition.
Verify both a prohibited new dependency and a permitted existing one. Update
examples and templates that would otherwise introduce fresh legacy usage.

A deprecation annotation is a signal until the configured tool makes it an
enforced rule. For Python, regular-build defaults often hide `DeprecationWarning`
outside `__main__`; `warnings.deprecated` was added in 3.13 and its runtime category
does not control static checker diagnostics. Inspect the installed checker,
warnings filters, and CI exit status before claiming enforcement. See the
[versioned warnings reference](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/warnings.html).

## Migrating consumers

Start with a batch whose compatibility check can reveal a missing replacement
behavior. Keep old/new interfaces available when supported consumers upgrade
independently. If persistent state changes, specify which versions can read and
write it during transition and recovery; restoring old code alone may not restore
compatibility. Name temporary adapters and their retirement dependencies.

For configuration or persisted-format changes, track readers separately from
writers, templates, and editors. Once a cohort can consume the replacement,
switch its producers/defaults and prevent new legacy adoption there; retain the
legacy path for cohorts still entitled to it. Each proposed batch needs a concrete
stop condition, the role that halts progression, and a bounded escalation point
if progress or recovery evidence is missing. Leave unassigned roles explicit.

Where policy differentiates advisory/soft deprecation from scheduled removal,
record that state explicitly. Python's [PEP 387](https://peps.python.org/pep-0387/)
is one such policy; its core-language and standard-library process does not set
grace periods for an unrelated application. Follow the target's actual support
agreement and version policy.

## Removing the old contract

Check the agreed policy, consumer transitions, retained-input requirements,
unresolved evidence, and recovery route before the removal step. Resolve residual
unknown consumers with the accountable decision owner; a calendar date cannot
silently accept that risk. Dry-run or rehearse against the actual packaging,
configuration, or routing boundary being removed. Keep an unaffected consumer
working while a deliberate legacy reference is detected by the intended check.

Record whether the old contract is merely hidden, disabled, or physically removed.
An adapter still required by a supported client is unfinished retirement work.
After an authorized removal, inspect the shipped boundary and exercise a legacy
use plus a supported control to establish what was actually removed. In a review
or plan, specify these post-release observations without claiming they ran.
Retire obsolete instructions, checks, and temporary resources only after their
remaining responsibilities are accounted for. Service shutdown, data disposal,
and public-product commitments need their own scoped procedures when applicable.

item.text:
**No-go for the October 1 removal as proposed.** Proceed with bounded preparation and migration work while retaining the supported v1 entrypoint, endpoint, and snapshot data. This decision uses the supplied **September 15, 2026** review date.

The maintenance benefit is clear, but the current state is advisory deprecation: existing consumers remain supported, no removal date was promised, and October 1 is explicitly unapproved. A README warning does not change those obligations. [Contract](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/contract.md:3), [release status](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/inventory.json:93)

**The proposal has five release blockers.**

1. **The replacement violates the audit contract.** V1 provides an immutable, complete period snapshot, including voided invoices, with stable IDs, values, order, and a shared snapshot identifier across pages. V2 reads a mutable collection, omits voided invoices, and provides no snapshot token. Collecting pages and filtering cannot recover those guarantees. The supplied example already loses `inv-2`, a voided invoice with `amount_minor: 200`, and has no snapshot identifier. Identical row schemas do not establish compatible behavior. [Contracts](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/contract.md:3), [sample](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/inventory.json:61)

2. **The absence evidence misses known consumers.** The September 8–15 gateway window falls between the August 31 and September 30 monthly runs. It establishes zero observed v1 calls through one authenticated gateway during that interval. The literal-symbol search establishes zero matches in three current default branches; it excludes the archived reporting image, templates, and ad-hoc installations, and does not establish absence of direct HTTP callers. [Evidence scope](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/contract.md:20), [inventory](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/inventory.json:39)

3. **Ownership and adoption controls are incomplete.** Reporting and template migrations have no assignees; ad-hoc installations have neither an owner nor an inventory. Leaving the generator unchanged creates new dependencies, while immediately rejecting every v1 import disrupts supported existing jobs. [Consumers and assignments](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/inventory.json:5), [proposed controls](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/proposal.md:9)

4. **The recovery plan destroys required recovery inputs.** Restoring an API binary cannot reconstruct deleted immutable snapshots from the mutable v2 collection. Retain the data and demonstrate historical replay and restoration. Any later data disposal needs a separate retention decision consistent with the audit requirement. [Audit requirement](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/contract.md:17), [proposed recovery](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/proposal.md:14)

5. **The completion criterion is insufficient.** A merged deletion PR proves neither a shipped removal nor successful consumer transitions. Also clarify “complete library” removal: the stated target is the v1 entrypoint and endpoint; the library also supplies `scan_v2()`. [Proposal](/tmp/tal-deprecation-trials-20260929/04-positive-r2/workspace/project/proposal.md:3)

The consumer disposition is:

| Consumer | Supported conclusion | Required next transition |
|---|---|---|
| Interactive dashboard | V2 rollout and current/nonvoided semantics are accepted; release captain is identified. | Keep as a regression control. Its acceptance does not cover audit exports. |
| Month-end close-audit | Known v1 dependency in an archived executable image; replacement behavior fails and no rehearsal exists. | Assign a migration owner; supply snapshot-capable behavior and prove historical reproduction. |
| Batch-job template | Still generates new v1 imports; owner team exists but no assignee. | Update generation defaults for compatible workloads; prevent unsupported audit workloads from silently selecting v2. |
| Ad-hoc installations and unenumerated HTTP callers | Dependency status remains unknown. | Assign discovery responsibility and establish coverage; unresolved exposure remains a removal gate. |

**Proposed bounded sequence for owning-team review**

These checkpoints are proposals, not accepted assignments or removal commitments. The ledger service owner owns the removal decision. At each missed gate, that role should stop dependent retirement work and resolve the blocker; v1 remains available.

1. **By September 16: establish accountability and scope.** Ledger platform maintainers and the service owner should secure accepted assignees from financial reporting and developer productivity, plus an owner for consumer discovery. Record supported client versions, compatibility/notice requirements, and any authority needed to change audit requirements. Keep unaccepted assignments explicitly pending. Limit the first migration batch to the known reporting job and generator.

2. **By September 18: close new-adoption paths and improve discovery.** Developer productivity, with ledger maintainers, should update the template and examples, then introduce checks scoped to **new** legacy dependencies. Existing supported reporting use needs a tracked exception with an owner and exit condition. Acceptance requires generated-project inspection, a deliberately prohibited new dependency that fails, and permitted existing usage that passes. Separately inspect archived job artifacts, configuration, direct endpoint references, and available installation records. State each check’s coverage; an import check does not cover HTTP callers.

3. **By September 22: review replacement readiness.** Ledger maintainers and the proposed reporting assignee should assess a snapshot-capable replacement using `close-2026-08-synthetic`; no need to wait for month end. Exercise the actual reporting consumer and verify complete rows including voids, stable ordering and values, consistent pagination, repeatability after collection changes, and historical replay. Inventory caller-required errors and retry behavior, which the supplied evidence does not describe. Current v2 fails this gate. If an adapter remains dependent on v1 or its storage, record that dependency as unfinished retirement work. A changed audit requirement needs explicit business approval, absent here.

4. **By September 25: review one-job migration and recovery evidence.** Only after replacement checks pass, rehearse the reporting job’s replacement artifact in isolation while both interfaces remain available. Verify restoration using retained code **and** snapshot data, including compatible readers and configuration. Preserve the previous job artifact for recovery. Financial reporting’s assignee and ledger maintainers should halt the pilot on any export mismatch or failed restore; no bulk migration follows automatically.

5. **September 30: reconcile the scheduled run.** Keep the existing supported path if earlier gates remain unmet. Otherwise, verify the migrated monthly job’s accepted output and execution artifact. Reconcile the inventory, exceptions, remaining HTTP dependencies, and gateway evidence around this actual run. One successful run does not close ad-hoc visibility gaps. October 1 remains a review checkpoint, not an automatic removal date.

6. **At a later evidence-backed release gate: rehearse, authorize, then verify removal.** Require completed consumer transitions, resolved or explicitly accepted residual unknown-consumer risk, satisfied support/notice obligations, and demonstrated recovery. In isolation, rehearse removal separately at the Python package and HTTP routing boundaries: deliberately exercise legacy use to prove detection, while a supported v2 consumer still works. Prepare notices with interfaces, replacement, transition, owner, and an approved date. After an authorized release, verify the shipped package and route behavior and surviving consumers. Report “ready to remove” separately from “removed”; defer snapshot disposal until its own obligations are resolved.

I inspected all four supplied files and compared the JSON samples locally. No executable migration, pagination, restoration, or removal rehearsal was available or run. All files remain unchanged; no services were called or communications sent.
